title: Tempdb Sort Spills
description: A large ORDER BY spills its sort to tempdb; an index that supplies the order removes the sort entirely. Why it matters: tempdb spills degrade every OTHER query sharing the server, not just the one spilling -- a classic, often misdiagnosed cause of "the whole server feels slow."
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Think about sorting a deck of cards. If you're sorting a hand of ten cards, you can just hold them all in your hands and shuffle them into order — easy, fast, all in your head. But if someone hands you ten thousand cards and tells you to sort them, you can't hold them all at once. You need to lay batches out on a table, sort each batch, and combine them — a slower, clunkier process that needs extra space beyond just your hands. This lesson is about the database equivalent of running out of "hands" (memory) while sorting, and having to spill the work out onto a "table" (disk).

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** When SQL Server runs a query with an `ORDER BY` (or certain other operations that need sorted data, like some joins and aggregations), it has to put the rows in order somehow. SQL Server estimates, in advance, roughly how much memory that sort will need, and requests that much memory before the query even starts running. If the estimate is right and the memory granted is enough, the sort happens entirely in memory — fast. But if there are more rows to sort than expected, or they're wider than expected, the memory granted runs out partway through, and SQL Server has to fall back to using disk space in `tempdb` (a special, shared, temporary work-space database that every query on the server can use) to hold the overflow. That fallback is called a "spill," and it turns a fast in-memory operation into a much slower one involving physical disk reads and writes.

**Why this happens in real databases.** The memory grant is decided before the query runs, based on the optimizer's row-count estimate. If that estimate is wrong — because statistics are stale, because the query has an unusual filter, or simply because the actual data has grown since the estimate was calculated — SQL Server can request too little memory. It has no way to "notice mid-flight" and ask for more; the grant is fixed for that execution. So a query that ran fine last month, when the table was smaller, can suddenly start spilling once the table crosses some size threshold, with no code change at all. This is one of the sneakier categories of performance regression, because nothing about the query text changed — only the data did.

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** When the optimizer builds a plan involving a sort, it estimates the number of rows and the average row width, multiplies them to guess the total data volume, and requests a chunk of memory (a "memory grant") sized to fit that estimate comfortably in RAM. The query then starts executing. If the actual number of rows flowing into the sort operator exceeds what fits in the granted memory, the sort operator can't just keep everything in RAM anymore. Instead, it writes what it currently has out to disk, in tempdb, as a temporary sorted run, frees up memory, and continues processing more rows the same way — building up a series of these sorted "runs" on disk. Once all the input has been consumed, it then has to merge all those separate sorted runs back together into one final sorted result, reading them back from disk. If you look at the actual execution plan for a query like this, the Sort operator will show warning icons and details under "Spill Details," including how many pages were spilled and how many spill passes it took — direct, visible evidence of the memory grant falling short.

**Why this matters in production — and why it's worse than it sounds.** A spill doesn't just make the one query slower, though it does — disk I/O is dramatically slower than RAM. The bigger problem is that tempdb is a single shared resource used by every query running on the entire server at that moment: other people's temp tables, other queries' own sorts and spills, version store data for snapshot isolation, all of it lives in the same tempdb. When one query spills a large sort into tempdb, it's generating extra I/O load and taking up space that competes with everything else happening on the server at the same time. A single badly-estimated query, spilling under load, can measurably slow down completely unrelated queries that happen to be sharing the same tempdb files. This is why experienced SQL Server practitioners watch for tempdb spills specifically as a "blast radius" problem, not just a "this one query is slow" problem.

The fix demonstrated in this lesson is to sidestep the sort entirely rather than trying to get the memory estimate more accurate: if there's an index whose key order already matches the `ORDER BY`, SQL Server can walk the index in that order and produce already-sorted output, with no separate sort step and therefore nothing to spill at all. You'll see the plan change from a Sort operator (with its spill warning) to a simple ordered Index Scan or Seek — the fastest possible way to satisfy an `ORDER BY`.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below runs a real `ORDER BY` against a sizeable table and shows you the actual execution plan SQL Server produces, including the spill warning details on the Sort operator if a spill occurs — the number of spilled pages and how many merge passes were needed to reassemble the final sorted output from disk. Once you add an index whose key order matches the `ORDER BY`, re-run the same query and compare the two plans side by side: the Sort operator (and its spill warning) disappears entirely, replaced by a simple ordered index access with none of tempdb's overhead involved at all.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** Sorts aren't the only operation that can spill to tempdb under a bad memory grant — hash joins and hash aggregates can spill in essentially the same way, for the same underlying reason (an estimate that undershoots the actual data volume). Whenever you see a query that used to be fast suddenly slow down with no code change, and the table it touches has grown substantially, a spilling operator anywhere in the plan — not just a Sort — is worth checking for specifically, since the fix (better estimates, or restructuring to avoid the operator entirely) is usually the same regardless of which operator is spilling.

## Scenario
`SELECT TOP (2000) ... FROM Events ORDER BY Amount` on a 500k-row table is slow and hammers tempdb. The plan has a **Sort** operator with a spill warning.

## Why it's slow
There is no index on `Amount`, so SQL Server must **sort** all qualifying rows at run time. A sort needs a **memory grant**; when the grant is too small for the data volume, the sort **spills to tempdb** — writing and re-reading pages on disk. Spills show as a warning on the Sort operator and as tempdb worktable I/O. Wide rows (the 200-char `Payload`) make it worse.

## What to look for
- A **Sort** operator, often with a **spill** warning (Sort Warnings).
- Worktable/workfile activity in `STATISTICS IO` (tempdb).

## The concept
The cheapest sort is the one you never do. An index on `Amount` stores rows in order, so the optimizer reads them pre-sorted and removes the **Sort** entirely — no memory grant, no tempdb spill. (When a sort is unavoidable, fixing the cardinality estimate so the grant is right is the other lever.)
startingQuery: SELECT TOP (2000) EventId, UserId, Amount FROM Events ORDER BY Amount, EventId OPTION (MAX_GRANT_PERCENT = 1);
hints: The Sort operator has a warning — what is it spilling to?
There is no index providing Amount order, so SQL Server sorts at run time and spills to tempdb.
Create a nonclustered index on Amount so rows arrive pre-sorted, the Sort disappears, and the plan reads the top rows straight from the index (drop the grant hint too).
